title: RankFormer: Rethinking Time Series Transformers through Representation Capacity Analysis and Progressive Decoding

paper.title: RankFormer: Rethinking Time Series Transformers through Representation Capacity Analysis and Progressive Decoding
paper.abstract:
Abstract. Multivariate time series forecasting plays a critical role in Web and
cyber-physical systems, where large-scale services and IoT infrastructures
generate complex temporal data. Transformer-based models have achieved strong empirical performance in this domain, yet the principles governing the expressive
capacity of their learned representations remain insufficiently understood.
Moreover, many existing models rely on simplified decoding strategies,
including channel-independent modeling and direct projection heads, which
limit their ability to capture complex multivariate dynamics.
To address these challenges, we propose RankFormer , a novel
encoder-decoder architecture for multivariate time series forecasting.
We establish a rank-based analysis framework to investigate how
tokenization, embedding, and attention designs affect the representation
capacity of time series Transformers. Our analysis reveals that
patchification increases the potential representation capacity by
aggregating multiple temporal observations into each token, while subsequent
encoding operations determine how much of this capacity is realized. Guided
by these insights, we develop a rank-enhancing encoder with Hourglass
Attention to improve rank stability during information interaction.
Furthermore, we introduce the Interactive Progressive Decoder
(IPD), which improves future trajectory modeling through global-guided
cross-channel interaction and progressive refinement.
Extensive experiments
on real-world long-term forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that RankFormer
achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art methods.
Code repository: https://github.com/TangPeiwang/Rankformer .

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Multivariate time series forecasting is a core problem in modern Web and cyber-physical systems. The growing integration of online services and IoT devices produces large volumes of continuously evolving sensor data ( Zhang et al., 2026e ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) , supporting applications such as server load balancing, traffic prediction, and resource planning ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026d ; Zhang et al., 2026c ) , as well as broader domains including finance, power systems, and transportation ( Zhou et al., 2021 ; Wu et al., 2021 ; Fang et al., 2025 ) . Transformer-based models have achieved substantial progress in time series forecasting owing to their ability to capture long-range dependencies ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2022 ; Zhou et al., 2022 ) . Recent architectural advances, including patch-based tokenization and specialized attention mechanisms, have further improved forecasting performance across diverse benchmarks ( Liu et al., 2024b ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . However, despite this empirical success, the underlying principles that determine the representation capacity of time series Transformers and their ability to translate learned representations into accurate forecasts remain insufficiently understood. (a) (b) Figure 1 . Empirical validation of rank stability and Hourglass Attention (HgA). (a) Rapid singular value decay shows bidirectional attention induces deep-layer rank collapse, while causal masking preserves representational diversity. (b) Causal masking restricts early tokens (starvation). In contrast, HgA uses a symmetric prefix as a global hub, enabling efficient context retrieval while maintaining rank stability. This limited understanding raises two fundamental questions: First, how do encoder architectures create and preserve expressive representations? Existing time series Transformers improve representation capability through various encoding designs, including tokenization, embedding, and attention mechanisms, yet how these components jointly shape the capacity of learned temporal representations remains insufficiently understood. Patchification provides a representative example: by aggregating multiple temporal observations into each token, it expands the attainable representation space compared with point-wise tokenization. However, the realized representation capacity is further shaped by subsequent encoding operations. Linear embeddings introduce rank constraints, while bidirectional attention (BiA) may cause excessive token mixing and representation homogenization, leading to rank degeneration ( Noci et al., 2022 ; Saada et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2021 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . Although unidirectional attention provides stronger rank stability, its restricted receptive field limits global information interaction. Consequently, existing attention designs struggle to simultaneously maintain representation diversity and achieve effective cross-token information exchange, limiting the ability of time series Transformers to fully exploit their representation space. Second, how can forecasting decoders fully exploit the learned representations? Although modern encoders can produce increasingly expressive latent features, many existing forecasting architectures still rely on simplified decoding strategies. Channel-independent modeling limits cross-variable interaction, while one-shot projection heads such as Flatten-Linear map encoded representations to the entire prediction horizon through a fixed transformation. Such designs overlook the evolving temporal organization and provide limited capability for progressively refining complex future trajectories, which is particularly restrictive for multivariate forecasting with strong cross-channel dependencies. To address these challenges, we propose RankFormer , a principled encoder-decoder architecture for multivariate time series forecasting. For the encoder, we establish a rank-based analysis framework to analyze how patchification, embedding, and attention topology shape the effective capacity of learned temporal representations. Based on these observations, we introduce Hourglass Attention (HgA) to improve rank stability during attention-based interaction, preserving diverse representations while enabling effective global information exchange. For the decoder, we develop an Interactive Progressive Decoder (IPD), which enhances future trajectory generation through global-context-guided cross-channel interaction and progressive refinement. Together, RankFormer provides a principled approach to improving representation learning and future trajectory modeling in time series Transformers. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We provide a rank-based analysis of time series Transformer encoders, revealing how patchification, embedding, and attention operations affect representation capacity and offering a theoretical explanation for the effectiveness of patch-based modeling. • We propose RankFormer , consisting of HgA and IPD. HgA preserves expressive representations through improved attention design, while IPD captures cross-channel dependencies and progressively refines future trajectories. • Extensive experiments on widely used long-term forecasting benchmarks validate the theoretical observations and demonstrate consistently strong performance against competitive state-of-the-art methods. Figure 2 . Overall structure of RankFormer. The model preprocesses multivariate time series via Instance Norm and CI, utilizing Patch Embedding and a Multi-Head Hourglass Attention encoder to generate a base prediction. An Interactive Progressive Decoder then refines these features. It trains via one-step residual learning using randomized partial ground truth, while inference employs a T T -step progressive refinement from a zero-residual state, concluding with Instance Denorm.

sections.heading: 2. Rank Theory Analysis and Key Theorems
sections.text: In this section, we establish a rank-based theoretical framework to analyze the core components of time series Transformers. We consider the forecasting problem as learning a mapping from historical observations 𝐗 ∈ ℝ L × C \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times C} to future sequences 𝐘 ∈ ℝ τ × C \mathbf{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{\tau\times C} . The model first transforms the input sequence into hidden representations 𝐇 ∈ ℝ N × D \mathbf{H}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D} , whose structure determines how much independent information can be preserved for subsequent forecasting. We use matrix rank, rank ⁡ ( 𝐇 ) \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{H}) , as a quantitative measure to characterize the independent information capacity of hidden representations. A higher rank indicates more independent representation directions and greater potential to preserve diverse information, whereas rank degradation suggests increased redundancy and reduced representation diversity.

sections.heading: 2.1. Patching as a Rank Expansion Mechanism
sections.text: When a univariate sequence 𝐱 ∈ ℝ L \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{L} is represented through point-wise tokenization, the resulting token matrix has a single feature dimension, and any linear embedding inherits a rank upper bound of one: rank ⁡ ( 𝐱 ⊤ ​ 𝐖 ) ≤ rank ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) ≤ 1 . \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{W})\leq\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{x})\leq 1. Proposition 0 (Rank Expansion via Patching). Partitioning 𝐱 \mathbf{x} into patches of length P P and arranging them into a patch matrix 𝐗 p ∈ ℝ N × P \mathbf{X}_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times P} , where N = ⌊ L / P ⌋ N=\lfloor L/P\rfloor , gives the attainable rank upper bound: rank ⁡ ( 𝐗 p ) ≤ min ⁡ ( N , P ) . \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}_{p})\leq\min(N,P). When P > 1 P>1 , patching expands the maximum attainable rank bound from one to min ⁡ ( N , P ) \min(N,P) , increasing the potential number of independent directions available for subsequent representation learning. This provides a rank-based perspective for understanding the effectiveness of patch-based modeling in time series Transformers.

sections.heading: 2.2. Embedding Layer: Breaking Linear Rank Constraints
sections.text: To map the patched representation 𝐗 p \mathbf{X}_{p} into a hidden representation 𝐇 ∈ ℝ N × D \mathbf{H}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D} , standard linear projections ( 𝐇 = 𝐗 p ​ 𝐖 \mathbf{H}=\mathbf{X}_{p}\mathbf{W} ) preserve the rank constraint of the input representation: rank ⁡ ( 𝐇 ) ≤ min ⁡ ( rank ⁡ ( 𝐗 p ) , D ) ≤ min ⁡ ( N , P , D ) . \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{H})\leq\min(\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}_{p}),D)\leq\min(N,P,D). When D > P D>P , linear embeddings remain constrained by the patch-induced rank bound, limiting the number of independent directions that can be represented in the hidden space. To overcome this linear rank constraint, we consider nonlinear MLP embeddings: 𝐇 = ϕ ⁡ ( 𝐗 p ​ 𝐖 1 + 𝐛 1 ) ​ 𝐖 2 + 𝐛 2 . \mathbf{H}=\phi(\mathbf{X}_{p}\mathbf{W}_{1}+\mathbf{b}_{1})\mathbf{W}_{2}+\mathbf{b}_{2}. Theorem 2 (Maximum Rank Embedding). Let ϕ \phi be a continuous, non-polynomial activation function. For any N N distinct input patches 𝐗 p ∈ ℝ N × P \mathbf{X}_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times P} , there exist MLP parameters such that the resulting hidden representation achieves the maximum attainable rank: rank ⁡ ( 𝐇 ) = min ⁡ ( N , D ) . \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{H})=\min(N,D). This theorem shows that nonlinear embeddings overcome the additional rank restriction imposed by linear projections, allowing hidden representations to achieve their maximum attainable rank determined by the sample and hidden dimensions. sections.heading: 2.3. Attention Mechanisms: Rank Preservation via Attention Topology
sections.text: BiA enables global information aggregation across tokens, but its dense mixing structure does not provide an explicit guarantee for preserving representation rank. Repeated dense token mixing may lead to representation homogenization and rank degradation in deep networks ( Noci et al., 2022 ; Saada et al., 2025 ) . To analyze how attention topology affects rank stability, we compare BiA with unidirectional (e.g., causal) attention. Let 𝐀 bid \mathbf{A}_{\textup{bid}} and 𝐀 causal \mathbf{A}_{\textup{causal}} denote their attention weight matrices, and let 𝐎 bid \mathbf{O}_{\textup{bid}} and 𝐎 causal \mathbf{O}_{\textup{causal}} denote the corresponding outputs after value projection and output projection. Theorem 3 (Rank Preservation of Causal Attention). Given identical projection parameters ( 𝐖 Q , 𝐖 K , 𝐖 V , 𝐖 O \mathbf{W}_{Q},\mathbf{W}_{K},\mathbf{W}_{V},\mathbf{W}^{O} ), causal attention preserves the rank of the value representation and guarantees: rank ⁡ ( 𝐎 causal ) ≥ rank ⁡ ( 𝐎 bid ) . \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{O}_{\textup{causal}})\geq\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{O}_{\textup{bid}}). Theorem 3 establishes that causal masking provides a structural rank-preservation property during attention aggregation. In contrast, BiA may reduce output rank when its learned aggregation fails to preserve independent information directions in the value representation (as shown in Figure 1 (a)). This analysis highlights the importance of attention topology in maintaining diverse representations during token interaction. Rather than favoring a specific topology, it motivates attention designs that preserve rank stability while enabling effective information exchange, leading to our proposed Hourglass Attention.

sections.heading: 3. RankFormer
sections.text: Guided by the rank-based theoretical framework established above, we propose RankFormer , as illustrated in Figure 2 . The architecture consists of a rank-guided encoder with HgA, which improves rank stability during attention-based interaction, and an IPD, which captures complex future trajectories through global-context-guided cross-channel interaction and progressive refinement.

sections.heading: 3.1. Patch Embedding
sections.text: To mitigate the adverse effects of magnitude variations across different variables, we first apply standard instance normalization to the input sequence 𝐗 \mathbf{X} along the temporal dimension. The normalized time series is then partitioned into patches of length P P , transforming the input into 𝐗 patches ∈ ℝ C × N × P \mathbf{X}_{\text{patches}}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times N\times P} , where N N is the number of patches. As elucidated in Proposition 1 , this patching operation structurally expands the rank capacity of the input representation. Subsequently, to break the inherent rank bound of linear projections, we map these patches into the hidden space ℝ D \mathbb{R}^{D} using a two-layer MLP with a ReLU activation ( Nair and Hinton, 2010 ) : 𝐇 embed = ReLU ​ ( 𝐗 patches ​ 𝐖 1 + 𝐛 1 ) ​ 𝐖 2 + 𝐛 2 \mathbf{H}_{\text{embed}}=\text{ReLU}(\mathbf{X}_{\text{patches}}\mathbf{W}_{1}+\mathbf{b}_{1})\mathbf{W}_{2}+\mathbf{b}_{2} where 𝐖 1 ∈ ℝ P × D mid \mathbf{W}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{P\times D_{\text{mid}}} and 𝐖 2 ∈ ℝ D mid × D \mathbf{W}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{\text{mid}}\times D} . As mathematically guaranteed by Theorem 2 , this nonlinear formulation ensures that the embedding achieves the theoretical maximum rank of min ⁡ ( N , D ) \min(N,D) , fully utilizing the representational potential of the high-dimensional hidden space.

sections.heading: 3.2. Hourglass Attention
sections.text: BiA enables global information aggregation across tokens, but repeated dense mixing may cause representation homogenization and rank degradation in deep networks. In contrast, causal attention provides a structural rank-preservation guarantee through its triangular topology, but its directional information flow limits efficient context exchange across tokens. To combine these complementary properties, we propose HgA, a topology-aware attention mechanism that reorganizes causal connectivity to maintain rank stability while enabling more effective information interaction. HgA introduces an hourglass-shaped attention topology through three design principles. First, early tokens are assigned broader receptive fields to aggregate global context from the observed sequence. Second, intermediate tokens use restricted receptive fields to reduce excessive token mixing and maintain representation diversity. Third, receptive fields gradually expand toward later tokens, preserving detailed recent information for downstream forecasting. Together, these designs redistribute information access within the sequence while retaining the rank-stability property inherited from causal attention. HgA is constructed by a topology-preserving reordering of causal attention. For an input sequence of length N N , we define ρ ⁡ ( i ) \rho(i) as the maximum visible key index of query position i i under this reordering: (1) ρ ⁡ ( i ) = { max ⁡ ( N − 2 − 2 ​ i , 0 ) , i ≤ ⌊ ( N − 1 ) / 2 ⌋ , 2 ​ i − N + 1 , i > ⌊ ( N − 1 ) / 2 ⌋ . \rho(i)=\begin{cases}\max(N-2-2i,0),&i\leq\lfloor(N-1)/2\rfloor,\\ 2i-N+1,&i>\lfloor(N-1)/2\rfloor.\end{cases} This mapping creates an hourglass-shaped receptive field: the visible range contracts toward the sequence center and expands toward the sequence end. The corresponding mask is: (2) 𝐌 Hg ​ [ i , j ] = { 0 , j ≤ ρ ⁡ ( i ) , − ∞ , otherwise . \mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{Hg}}[i,j]=\begin{cases}0,&j\leq\rho(i),\\ -\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} The attention operation is: (3) 𝐀 Hg = Softmax ⁡ ( 𝐐𝐊 ⊤ d k + 𝐌 Hg ) , \mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{Hg}}=\operatorname{Softmax}\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}+\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{Hg}}\right), (4) HgAttn ⁡ ( 𝐐 , 𝐊 , 𝐕 ) = 𝐀 Hg ​ 𝐕 . \operatorname{HgAttn}(\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{K},\mathbf{V})=\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{Hg}}\mathbf{V}. Since HgA is obtained through a reordering of causal connectivity, its attention matrix retains the rank-preservation property of causal attention while providing a different receptive field allocation.

sections.heading: 3.3. Interactive Progressive Decoder
sections.text: The IPD (Figure 3 ) addresses the mapping bottleneck by transforming channel-independent encoder representations into multivariate forecasts. It first generates a channel-wise base prediction, then introduces cross-channel conditioning to incorporate interactions among variables, and finally refines the prediction through progressive residual updates.

A learnable channel embedding 𝐞 C \mathbf{e}_{C} is combined with the prediction feature: (6) 𝐟 C = [ 𝐮 C ; 𝐞 C ] , \mathbf{f}_{C}=[\mathbf{u}_{C};\mathbf{e}_{C}], where 𝐟 C \mathbf{f}_{C} represents the channel-specific conditioning feature. sections.text: During inference, IPD initializes the prediction state as 𝐲 C ( 0 ) = 𝟎 \mathbf{y}_{C}^{(0)}=\mathbf{0} and performs T T residual updates: (14) 𝐲 C ( t ) = 𝐲 C ( t − 1 ) + 1 T ( 𝐖 state 𝐲 C ( t − 1 ) + 𝐖 cond 𝐲 C cond + 𝐛 ) , t = 1 , … , T . \mathbf{y}_{C}^{(t)}=\mathbf{y}_{C}^{(t-1)}+\frac{1}{T}\left(\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{state}}\mathbf{y}_{C}^{(t-1)}+\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{cond}}\mathbf{y}_{C}^{\mathrm{cond}}+\mathbf{b}\right),\quad t=1,\ldots,T. Since the residual update is affine in the prediction state and 𝐲 C cond \mathbf{y}_{C}^{\mathrm{cond}} remains fixed across iterations, the T T updates can be analytically combined. Specifically, defining (15) 𝐒 T = 1 T ​ ∑ k = 0 T − 1 ( 𝐈 + 𝐖 state T ) k , \mathbf{S}_{T}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\left(\mathbf{I}+\frac{\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{state}}}{T}\right)^{k}, the final prediction becomes (16) 𝐲 C ( T ) = 𝐁 eff ​ 𝐲 C cond + 𝐛 eff , \mathbf{y}_{C}^{(T)}=\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{eff}}\mathbf{y}_{C}^{\mathrm{cond}}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{eff}}, where 𝐁 eff = 𝐒 T ​ 𝐖 cond \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{eff}}=\mathbf{S}_{T}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{cond}} and 𝐛 eff = 𝐒 T ​ 𝐛 \mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{eff}}=\mathbf{S}_{T}\mathbf{b} . These equivalent parameters are precomputed after training, allowing IPD to reproduce the progressive refinement through a single affine mapping during inference.

sections.heading: 4. Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate RankFormer on diverse real-world long-term time series forecasting benchmarks spanning Web- and IoT-relevant applications, demonstrating its superior representational capacity and stable progressive decoding against state-of-the-art (SOTA) baselines.

sections.heading: Datasets.
sections.text: We evaluate our model on nine widely adopted real-world benchmarks: Electricity, Traffic, Weather, Exchange-Rate, Solar, and four ETT datasets (ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2). These datasets cover diverse applications relevant to Web and IoT systems, including transportation, energy management, and environmental monitoring, alongside financial forecasting.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We benchmark RankFormer against 9 recent SOTA forecasting models. To ensure a comprehensive evaluation, these baselines encompass advanced Transformer-based architectures (SEER ( Qiu et al., 2026 ) , iTransformer ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , PatchTST ( Nie et al., 2023 ) , Fredformer ( Piao et al., 2024 ) ), linear-centric networks (DLinear ( Zeng et al., 2023 ) ), and other highly competitive contemporary approaches (SRSNet ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , DUET ( Qiu et al., 2025 ) , xPatch ( Stitsyuk and Choi, 2025 ) , Amplifier ( Fei et al., 2025 ) ).

sections.heading: Experimental Setup.
sections.text: We evaluate all models under standard long-term forecasting settings, τ ∈ { 96,192,336,720 } \tau\in\{96,192,336,720\} . Performance is measured by Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE). Baseline results are taken from original publications or reproduced using official implementations under the same settings.

sections.heading: 4.1. Main Results
sections.text: As shown in Table 1 , we evaluate the long-term forecasting performance of RankFormer against SOTA baselines. All models use a fixed input sequence length of 96, with results averaged across four forecasting horizons. RankFormer demonstrates comprehensive superiority, achieving the best MSE and MAE on 7 out of 8 benchmark datasets (securing 14 out of 16 top metrics). While the recent SEER model shows competitive performance and achieves the best results on the Traffic dataset, RankFormer maintains a strong second place with marginal differences. Compared with established baselines such as PatchTST and iTransformer, RankFormer achieves lower forecasting errors across diverse applications relevant to Web and IoT systems, including energy management (Solar) and environmental monitoring (Weather). These results demonstrate the strong and consistent forecasting performance of RankFormer across diverse real-world scenarios.

sections.heading: 4.2.1. Predictive Value of Embedding Rank Expansion
sections.text: We construct synthetic targets with controlled rank to evaluate the predictive benefit of nonlinear embeddings. We compare linear, parameter-matched affine, and MLP embeddings using identical attention and prediction heads that preserve the embedding rank constraints. Both affine embeddings have a rank upper bound of five. Figure 4 (a) shows comparable performance at target rank 4. At higher target ranks, the MLP achieves MSE below the rank-five lower bound, while affine embeddings remain constrained. In (b), increasing the contribution of higher-rank target components substantially degrades the rank-constrained MLP, whereas the unconstrained MLP maintains stable performance. These results demonstrate that nonlinear embeddings can exploit higher attainable rank to improve prediction when target structures exceed the linear rank constraint.

sections.heading: 4.2.2. Impact of Representation Rank Constraints
sections.text: To investigate the impact of representation rank constraints on forecasting, we impose rank limits of 1, 4, and 8 on position-enriched patch representations in a standard Transformer encoder. The constraints are maintained during training and inference, with all other settings unchanged. sections.heading: 5. Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we present RankFormer, a principled encoder-decoder architecture for multivariate time series forecasting. Through a rank-based analytical framework, we revisit how tokenization, embedding, and attention designs influence the capacity of learned representations. Our analysis reveals that patchification expands the attainable rank bound, nonlinear embeddings overcome the additional constraints of linear projections, and attention topology plays an important role in preserving representation diversity during information interaction. Guided by these insights, we develop a rank-enhancing encoder with HgA and an IPD, which respectively improve representation preservation and future trajectory modeling through effective information exchange and progressive refinement. Extensive experiments on real-world forecasting benchmarks validate the effectiveness of RankFormer and demonstrate consistent improvements over competitive methods.

sections.heading: A.1. Time Series Forecasting
sections.text: Time series forecasting faces challenges in modeling long-term dependencies and complex dynamics. Traditional RNNs and CNNs suffer from scalability bottlenecks and difficulties in handling long sequences ( Cheng et al., 2020 ; Salinas et al., 2020 ) . In contrast, Transformers have achieved superior performance by leveraging self-attention mechanisms, spurring the development of efficient and interpretable temporal models ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) such as Informer ( Zhou et al., 2021 ) , Autoformer ( Wu et al., 2021 ) , and PatchTST ( Nie et al., 2023 ) . Meanwhile, frequency-domain methods effectively capture periodic and spectral patterns in time series through Fourier or wavelet transforms ( Murad et al., 2025 ) . Representative works, including Fredformer ( Piao et al., 2024 ) , FreTS ( Yi et al., 2023 ) , and FITS ( Xu et al., 2024 ) , demonstrate competitive advantages in extracting global features. Recent studies further integrate temporal and frequency-domain information, proposing hybrid modeling approaches. For example, CDX-Net combines multiple network structures for feature fusion ( Li et al., 2022 ) , FEDformer unifies decomposition and frequency analysis ( Zhou et al., 2022 ) , and TimeMixer++ enhances temporal representation through multi-scale sampling and attention mechanisms, advancing the field ( Wang et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: A.2. Rank Analysis in Transformer
sections.text: Low-rank attention research aims to improve Transformer efficiency through low-rank approximations or parameterization. Low-rank approximation methods, such as Linformer ( Wang et al., 2020 ) , Nystromformer ( Xiong et al., 2021 ) , and Performer ( Choromanski et al., 2021 ) , utilize low-dimensional projections, anchor tokens, or random feature mappings to reduce attention computational complexity to linear. Low-rank parameterization methods ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Hayou et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024a ) , directly learn low-rank update matrices for efficient fine-tuning but lack theoretical guidance on the underlying causes of low-rank behavior. Theoretical analysis reveals that pure attention networks suffer from a double-exponential collapse in representation rank as depth increases, a phenomenon known as rank collapse ( Noci et al., 2022 ; Saada et al., 2025 ) . Studies indicate that residual connections, layer normalization, and feed-forward networks can effectively mitigate this issue and maintain representational diversity ( Dong et al., 2021 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) . Additionally, the relationship between attention head dimension and sequence length influences the rank of attention matrices, thereby constraining model expressiveness ( Bhojanapalli et al., 2020 ) . In time series forecasting, sequence embeddings exhibit rapidly decaying singular value spectra, naturally concentrating in low-rank subspaces and endowing attention layers with inherent compressibility ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . However, existing work still lacks a unified theoretical framework to systematically guide the overall design and optimization of time series Transformers from a rank perspective.

Given query, key, and value projections: 𝐐 = 𝐗𝐖 Q , 𝐊 = 𝐗𝐖 K , 𝐕 = 𝐗𝐖 V , \mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_{Q},\quad\mathbf{K}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_{K},\quad\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_{V}, the attention output after output projection can be written as 𝐎 = 𝐀𝐗 V , \mathbf{O}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}_{V}, where 𝐗 V = 𝐕𝐖 O , \mathbf{X}_{V}=\mathbf{V}\mathbf{W}^{O}, and 𝐀 \mathbf{A} denotes the corresponding attention aggregation matrix. The following analysis focuses on whether the attention aggregation matrix 𝐀 \mathbf{A} preserves the rank of the value representation.

sections.heading: D.1. Full-rank Potential of Bidirectional Attention
sections.text: BiA is not inherently rank deficient. We show that its attention matrix can achieve full rank under suitable projection parameters. Given an input matrix 𝐗 \mathbf{X} with distinct rows, there exists a projection direction 𝐯 \mathbf{v} such that 𝐮 = 𝐗𝐯 \mathbf{u}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v} contains pairwise distinct values. Choosing one-dimensional query and key projections as 𝐐 = α ​ 𝐮 , 𝐊 = β ​ 𝐮 , \mathbf{Q}=\alpha\mathbf{u},\qquad\mathbf{K}=\beta\mathbf{u}, produces the attention score matrix 𝐒 = γ ​ 𝐮𝐮 ⊤ . \mathbf{S}=\gamma\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^{\top}. Although 𝐒 \mathbf{S} is rank one, the element-wise exponential matrix generated by the softmax operation, 𝐄 i ​ j = exp ⁡ ( γ ​ u i ​ u j ) , \mathbf{E}_{ij}=\exp(\gamma u_{i}u_{j}), is full rank for distinct { u i } \{u_{i}\} . Since the softmax normalization only introduces an invertible diagonal scaling, the resulting bidirectional attention matrix can achieve rank ⁡ ( 𝐀 bid ) = n . \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A}_{\textup{bid}})=n. Therefore, BiA itself does not suffer from an intrinsic rank limitation. Its limitation is the absence of a structural guarantee for preserving rank during repeated token interaction.

sections.heading: Different Patch Sizes
sections.text: As shown in Figure 14 , we systematically evaluated the singular value distribution of embedding matrices under different patch sizes (1, 4, 8, 16) across 7 datasets. The experimental results show that for most datasets, the singular value decay curves of their embedding representations generally exhibit full-rank or near-full-rank characteristics, even under the smallest patch size (1). This indicates that the model can learn highly diverse and linearly independent representations for these datasets, with their effective rank significantly surpassing the inherent bottleneck of the original univariate input (which has an upper rank bound of 1).

Multivariate time series forecasting plays a critical role in Web and cyber-physical systems, where large-scale services and IoT infrastructures generate complex temporal data. Transformer-based models have achieved strong empirical performance in this domain, yet the principles governing the expressive capacity of their learned representations remain insufficiently understood. Moreover, many existing models rely on simplified decoding strategies, including channel-independent modeling and direct projection heads, which limit their ability to capture complex multivariate dynamics. To address these challenges, we propose RankFormer , a novel encoder-decoder architecture for multivariate time series forecasting. We establish a rank-based analysis framework to investigate how tokenization, embedding, and attention designs affect the representation capacity of time series Transformers. Our analysis reveals that patchification increases the potential representation capacity by aggregating multiple temporal observations into each token, while subsequent encoding operations determine how much of this capacity is realized. Guided by these insights, we develop a rank-enhancing encoder with Hourglass Attention to improve rank stability during information interaction. Furthermore, we introduce the Interactive Progressive Decoder (IPD), which improves future trajectory modeling through global-guided cross-channel interaction and progressive refinement. Extensive experiments on real-world long-term forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that RankFormer achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art methods. Code repository: https://github.com/TangPeiwang/Rankformer . Keywords: Time Series, Representation Capacity, Hourglass Attention, Interactive Progressive Decoder 1. Introduction Multivariate time series forecasting is a core problem in modern Web and cyber-physical systems. The growing integration of online services and IoT devices produces large volumes of continuously evolving sensor data ( Zhang et al., 2026e ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) , supporting applications such as server load balancing, traffic prediction, and resource planning ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026d ; Zhang et al., 2026c ) , as well as broader domains including finance, power systems, and transportation ( Zhou et al., 2021 ; Wu et al., 2021 ; Fang et al., 2025 ) . Transformer-based models have achieved substantial progress in time series forecasting owing to their ability to capture long-range dependencies ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2022 ; Zhou et al., 2022 ) . Recent architectural advances, including patch-based tokenization and specialized attention mechanisms, have further improved forecasting performance across diverse benchmarks ( Liu et al., 2024b ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . However, despite this empirical success, the underlying principles that determine the representation capacity of time series Transformers and their ability to translate learned representations into accurate forecasts remain insufficiently understood. (a) (b) Figure 1 . Empirical validation of rank stability and Hourglass Attention (HgA). (a) Rapid singular value decay shows bidirectional attention induces deep-layer rank collapse, while causal masking preserves representational diversity. (b) Causal masking restricts early tokens (starvation). In contrast, HgA uses a symmetric prefix as a global hub, enabling efficient context retrieval while maintaining rank stability. This limited understanding raises two fundamental questions: First, how do encoder architectures create and preserve expressive representations? Existing time series Transformers improve representation capability through various encoding designs, including tokenization, embedding, and attention mechanisms, yet how these components jointly shape the capacity of learned temporal representations remains insufficiently understood. Patchification provides a representative example: by aggregating multiple temporal observations into each token, it expands the attainable representation space compared with point-wise tokenization. However, the realized representation capacity is further shaped by subsequent encoding operations. Linear embeddings introduce rank constraints, while bidirectional attention (BiA) may cause excessive token mixing and representation homogenization, leading to rank degeneration ( Noci et al., 2022 ; Saada et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2021 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . Although unidirectional attention provides stronger rank stability, its restricted receptive field limits global information interaction. Consequently, existing attention designs struggle to simultaneously maintain representation diversity and achieve effective cross-token information exchange, limiting the ability of time series Transformers to fully exploit their representation space. Second, how can forecasting decoders fully exploit the learned representations? Although modern encoders can produce increasingly expressive latent features, many existing forecasting architectures still rely on simplified decoding strategies. Channel-independent modeling limits cross-variable interaction, while one-shot projection heads such as Flatten-Linear map encoded representations to the entire prediction horizon through a fixed transformation. Such designs overlook the evolving temporal organization and provide limited capability for progressively refining complex future trajectories, which is particularly restrictive for multivariate forecasting with strong cross-channel dependencies. To address these challenges, we propose RankFormer , a principled encoder-decoder architecture for multivariate time series forecasting. For the encoder, we establish a rank-based analysis framework to analyze how patchification, embedding, and attention topology shape the effective capacity of learned temporal representations. Based on these observations, we introduce Hourglass Attention (HgA) to improve rank stability during attention-based interaction, preserving diverse representations while enabling effective global information exchange. For the decoder, we develop an Interactive Progressive Decoder (IPD), which enhances future trajectory generation through global-context-guided cross-channel interaction and progressive refinement. Together, RankFormer provides a principled approach to improving representation learning and future trajectory modeling in time series Transformers. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We provide a rank-based analysis of time series Transformer encoders, revealing how patchification, embedding, and attention operations affect representation capacity and offering a theoretical explanation for the effectiveness of patch-based modeling. • We propose RankFormer , consisting of HgA and IPD. HgA preserves expressive representations through improved attention design, while IPD captures cross-channel dependencies and progressively refines future trajectories. • Extensive experiments on widely used long-term forecasting benchmarks validate the theoretical observations and demonstrate consistently strong performance against competitive state-of-the-art methods. Rank Theory Analysis and Key Theorems In this section, we establish a rank-based theoretical framework to analyze the core components of time series Transformers. We consider the forecasting problem as learning a mapping from historical observations 𝐗 ∈ ℝ L × C \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times C} to future sequences 𝐘 ∈ ℝ τ × C \mathbf{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{\tau\times C} . The model first transforms the input sequence into hidden representations 𝐇 ∈ ℝ N × D \mathbf{H}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D} , whose structure determines how much independent information can be preserved for subsequent forecasting. We use matrix rank, rank ⁡ ( 𝐇 ) \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{H}) , as a quantitative measure to characterize the independent information capacity of hidden representations. A higher rank indicates more independent representation directions and greater potential to preserve diverse information, whereas rank degradation suggests increased redundancy and reduced representation diversity. 2.1. Patching as a Rank Expansion Mechanism When a univariate sequence 𝐱 ∈ ℝ L \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{L} is represented through point-wise tokenization, the resulting token matrix has a single feature dimension, and any linear embedding inherits a rank upper bound of one: rank ⁡ ( 𝐱 ⊤ ​ 𝐖 ) ≤ rank ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) ≤ 1 . \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{W})\leq\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{x})\leq 1. Proposition 0 (Rank Expansion via Patching). Partitioning 𝐱 \mathbf{x} into patches of length P P and arranging them into a patch matrix 𝐗 p ∈ ℝ N × P \mathbf{X}_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times P} , where N = ⌊ L / P ⌋ N=\lfloor L/P\rfloor , gives the attainable rank upper bound: rank ⁡ ( 𝐗 p ) ≤ min ⁡ ( N , P ) . \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}_{p})\leq\min(N,P). When P > 1 P>1 , patching expands the maximum attainable rank bound from one to min ⁡ ( N , P ) \min(N,P) , increasing the potential number of independent directions available for subsequent representation learning. This provides a rank-based perspective for understanding the effectiveness of patch-based modeling in time series Transformers. 2.2. Embedding Layer: Breaking Linear Rank Constraints To map the patched representation 𝐗 p \mathbf{X}_{p} into a hidden representation 𝐇 ∈ ℝ N × D \mathbf{H}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D} , standard linear projections ( 𝐇 = 𝐗 p ​ 𝐖 \mathbf{H}=\mathbf{X}_{p}\mathbf{W} ) preserve the rank constraint of the input representation: rank ⁡ ( 𝐇 ) ≤ min ⁡ ( rank ⁡ ( 𝐗 p ) , D ) ≤ min ⁡ ( N , P , D ) . \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{H})\leq\min(\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}_{p}),D)\leq\min(N,P,D). When D > P D>P , linear embeddings remain constrained by the patch-induced rank bound, limiting the number of independent directions that can be represented in the hidden space. To overcome this linear rank constraint, we consider nonlinear MLP embeddings: 𝐇 = ϕ ⁡ ( 𝐗 p ​ 𝐖 1 + 𝐛 1 ) ​ 𝐖 2 + 𝐛 2 . \mathbf{H}=\phi(\mathbf{X}_{p}\mathbf{W}_{1}+\mathbf{b}_{1})\mathbf{W}_{2}+\mathbf{b}_{2}. Theorem 2 (Maximum Rank Embedding). Let ϕ \phi be a continuous, non-polynomial activation function. For any N N distinct input patches 𝐗 p ∈ ℝ N × P \mathbf{X}_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times P} , there exist MLP parameters such that the resulting hidden representation achieves the maximum attainable rank: rank ⁡ ( 𝐇 ) = min ⁡ ( N , D ) . \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{H})=\min(N,D). This theorem shows that nonlinear embeddings overcome the additional rank restriction imposed by linear projections, allowing hidden representations to achieve their maximum attainable rank determined by the sample and hidden dimensions. Attention Mechanisms: Rank Preservation via Attention Topology BiA enables global information aggregation across tokens, but its dense mixing structure does not provide an explicit guarantee for preserving representation rank. Repeated dense token mixing may lead to representation homogenization and rank degradation in deep networks ( Noci et al., 2022 ; Saada et al., 2025 ) . To analyze how attention topology affects rank stability, we compare BiA with unidirectional (e.g., causal) attention. Let 𝐀 bid \mathbf{A}_{\textup{bid}} and 𝐀 causal \mathbf{A}_{\textup{causal}} denote their attention weight matrices, and let 𝐎 bid \mathbf{O}_{\textup{bid}} and 𝐎 causal \mathbf{O}_{\textup{causal}} denote the corresponding outputs after value projection and output projection. Theorem 3 (Rank Preservation of Causal Attention). Given identical projection parameters ( 𝐖 Q , 𝐖 K , 𝐖 V , 𝐖 O \mathbf{W}_{Q},\mathbf{W}_{K},\mathbf{W}_{V},\mathbf{W}^{O} ), causal attention preserves the rank of the value representation and guarantees: rank ⁡ ( 𝐎 causal ) ≥ rank ⁡ ( 𝐎 bid ) . \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{O}_{\textup{causal}})\geq\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{O}_{\textup{bid}}). Theorem 3 establishes that causal masking provides a structural rank-preservation property during attention aggregation. In contrast, BiA may reduce output rank when its learned aggregation fails to preserve independent information directions in the value representation (as shown in Figure 1 (a)). This analysis highlights the importance of attention topology in maintaining diverse representations during token interaction. Rather than favoring a specific topology, it motivates attention designs that preserve rank stability while enabling effective information exchange, leading to our proposed Hourglass Attention. 3. RankFormer Guided by the rank-based theoretical framework established above, we propose RankFormer , as illustrated in Figure 2 . The architecture consists of a rank-guided encoder with HgA, which improves rank stability during attention-based interaction, and an IPD, which captures complex future trajectories through global-context-guided cross-channel interaction and progressive refinement. 3.1. Patch Embedding To mitigate the adverse effects of magnitude variations across different variables, we first apply standard instance normalization to the input sequence 𝐗 \mathbf{X} along the temporal dimension. The normalized time series is then partitioned into patches of length P P , transforming the input into 𝐗 patches ∈ ℝ C × N × P \mathbf{X}_{\text{patches}}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times N\times P} , where N N is the number of patches. As elucidated in Proposition 1 , this patching operation structurally expands the rank capacity of the input representation. Subsequently, to break the inherent rank bound of linear projections, we map these patches into the hidden space ℝ D \mathbb{R}^{D} using a two-layer MLP with a ReLU activation ( Nair and Hinton, 2010 ) : 𝐇 embed = ReLU ​ ( 𝐗 patches ​ 𝐖 1 + 𝐛 1 ) ​ 𝐖 2 + 𝐛 2 \mathbf{H}_{\text{embed}}=\text{ReLU}(\mathbf{X}_{\text{patches}}\mathbf{W}_{1}+\mathbf{b}_{1})\mathbf{W}_{2}+\mathbf{b}_{2} where 𝐖 1 ∈ ℝ P × D mid \mathbf{W}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{P\times D_{\text{mid}}} and 𝐖 2 ∈ ℝ D mid × D \mathbf{W}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{\text{mid}}\times D} . As mathematically guaranteed by Theorem 2 , this nonlinear formulation ensures that the embedding achieves the theoretical maximum rank of min ⁡ ( N , D ) \min(N,D) , fully utilizing the representational potential of the high-dimensional hidden space. 3.2. Hourglass Attention BiA enables global information aggregation across tokens, but repeated dense mixing may cause representation homogenization and rank degradation in deep networks. In contrast, causal attention provides a structural rank-preservation guarantee through its triangular topology, but its directional information flow limits efficient context exchange across tokens. To combine these complementary properties, we propose HgA, a topology-aware attention mechanism that reorganizes causal connectivity to maintain rank stability while enabling more effective information interaction. HgA introduces an hourglass-shaped attention topology through three design principles. First, early tokens are assigned broader receptive fields to aggregate global context from the observed sequence. Second, intermediate tokens use restricted receptive fields to reduce excessive token mixing and maintain representation diversity. Third, receptive fields gradually expand toward later tokens, preserving detailed recent information for downstream forecasting. Together, these designs redistribute information access within the sequence while retaining the rank-stability property inherited from causal attention. HgA is constructed by a topology-preserving reordering of causal attention. For an input sequence of length N N , we define ρ ⁡ ( i ) \rho(i) as the maximum visible key index of query position i i under this reordering: (1) ρ ⁡ ( i ) = { max ⁡ ( N − 2 − 2 ​ i , 0 ) , i ≤ ⌊ ( N − 1 ) / 2 ⌋ , 2 ​ i − N + 1 , i > ⌊ ( N − 1 ) / 2 ⌋ . \rho(i)=\begin{cases}\max(N-2-2i,0),&i\leq\lfloor(N-1)/2\rfloor,\\ 2i-N+1,&i>\lfloor(N-1)/2\rfloor.\end{cases} This mapping creates an hourglass-shaped receptive field: the visible range contracts toward the sequence center and expands toward the sequence end. Since HgA is obtained through a reordering of causal connectivity, its attention matrix retains the rank-preservation property of causal attention while providing a different receptive field allocation. 3.3. Interactive Progressive Decoder The IPD (Figure 3 ) addresses the mapping bottleneck by transforming channel-independent encoder representations into multivariate forecasts. It first generates a channel-wise base prediction, then introduces cross-channel conditioning to incorporate interactions among variables, and finally refines the prediction through progressive residual updates. Experiments We evaluate RankFormer on diverse real-world long-term time series forecasting benchmarks spanning Web- and IoT-relevant applications, demonstrating its superior representational capacity and stable progressive decoding against state-of-the-art (SOTA) baselines. Conclusion In this paper, we present RankFormer, a principled encoder-decoder architecture for multivariate time series forecasting. Through a rank-based analytical framework, we revisit how tokenization, embedding, and attention designs influence the capacity of learned representations. Our analysis reveals that patchification expands the attainable rank bound, nonlinear embeddings overcome the additional constraints of linear projections, and attention topology plays an important role in preserving representation diversity during information interaction. Guided by these insights, we develop a rank-enhancing encoder with HgA and an IPD, which respectively improve representation preservation and future trajectory modeling through effective information exchange and progressive refinement.
